analysis.one_liner: Lets employees at companies with 50 or more workers take up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for a birth, adoption, or serious illness.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 253–177 on November 13, 1991, but the bill never became law before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have guaranteed employees at workplaces with at least 50 workers up to 12 workweeks of unpaid leave in a year to have or adopt a child, to care for a seriously ill child, spouse, or parent, or to deal with their own serious health condition. Their job (or an equivalent one) and their health insurance would be protected while they were out. The leave is unpaid unless the employee has paid leave to substitute, and the smallest employers are exempt. Congress's own findings say the bill responds to working parents — especially mothers — being forced to choose between job security and caring for family [S6].
analysis.who_benefits: Employees who have worked at least 12 months and 1,000 hours at an employer with 50 or more employees within 75 miles of their worksite: birth and adoptive parents, people caring for a seriously ill child, spouse, or parent, and workers facing their own serious illness. They could take up to 12 weeks off without losing their job, an equivalent position, or their health coverage [S2][S5].

how_it_helps.text: Entitles eligible employees to 12 workweeks of leave in any 12-month period for a birth, an adoption or foster placement, care of a seriously ill child, spouse, or parent, or their own serious health condition [S2][S5].

Requires the employer to restore the worker to the same or an equivalent position and to maintain group health coverage during the leave, so taking leave does not mean losing a job or insurance [S5][S6].

Makes it unlawful for an employer to interfere with these rights or to punish someone for filing a complaint or testifying, and lets workers sue, with wages, interest, and attorney's fees available [S6].
Extends similar protections to federal civil service employees and to House and Senate employees, including congressional staff [S2][S5][S6].

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers — private businesses and public agencies with 50 or more employees within 75 miles of a worksite — bear the cost of holding jobs open, maintaining health benefits, and scheduling around leave. The leave is unpaid, so employees also bear lost income unless they have paid leave to substitute [S2][S5][S6].

drawbacks.text: The leave is unpaid: the bill expressly does not require an employer to provide paid sick or medical leave it would not normally offer, so many workers cannot afford to use the right [S2][S5].

Workers at businesses with fewer than 50 employees within 75 miles — and those with less than 12 months or 1,000 hours on the job — get nothing, leaving out many low-wage and small-firm employees [S2][S5].
Spouses who work for the same employer may be limited to a combined 12 weeks for a birth, adoption, or care of a sick parent [S2][S6].
The highest-paid 10 percent of an employer's workforce can be denied their job back if the leave would cause the employer substantial and grievous economic injury [S5][S6].

Covered employers face real compliance costs — holding positions and paying health premiums during leave, certifying and sometimes second-guessing medical claims, and scheduling around absences — an objection that is strongest for firms just over the 50-employee line [S5][S6].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a deliberately modest guarantee: unpaid leave with job and health-insurance protection, scoped to larger employers, with medical certification requirements, notice rules, and special accommodations for teachers. Its chief weakness is that unpaid leave is only real help for families who can afford 12 weeks without a paycheck — which the bill itself acknowledged by creating a commission to study salary replacement [S6]. Critics' concerns about disruption and cost for employers near the size threshold were taken seriously in the design, but the core benefit to workers facing a birth, an adoption, or a serious illness is substantial and comes at a genuine but bounded cost to covered employers.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by a wide bipartisan margin in November 1991, then laid its own action aside in favor of a Senate companion bill — and no law resulted before this Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. William Clay introduced the Family and Medical Leave Act of 1991 on January 3, 1991, as the first bill of the 102nd Congress, with original cosponsors including both Democrats and Republicans such as Rep. Marge Roukema [S6].
The bill was referred to three committees; the Education and Labor Committee and the Post Office and Civil Service Committee both reported it amended on June 27, 1991 [S3][S4][S8].
On November 12, 1991, the Rules Committee reported a rule allowing floor debate with only specified amendments in order [S8].
On November 13, 1991, a motion to recommit the bill with instructions — a last attempt to send it back to committee for changes — failed 119–312 [S8][S9].
The House passed the bill 253–177, with 217 of 267 Democrats and 35 of 166 Republicans voting yes [S8][S10].
The House then laid the bill on the table with a reference to S. 5 for further action, and the bill was not enacted before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S8].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers over the 50-employee threshold are better off, since they never had to hold jobs and health benefits open for 12 weeks of family and medical leave. Workers who needed that leave — new parents and people caring for seriously ill family members — got nothing in this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Passage was bipartisan in absolute numbers — 217 of 267 Democrats and 35 of 166 Republicans voted yes — but opposition was heavily Republican, with 129 of 166 Republicans and only 48 of 267 Democrats voting no; the failed motion to recommit split 16 Democrats for to 250 against, and 103 Republicans for to 61 against [S9][S10].

industries.industry: Employers with 50 or more employees (including public agencies)
industries.note: They would have had to hold jobs open for up to 12 weeks, maintain health coverage during leave, and allow reinstatement, with damages and attorney's fees for violations. Workers at those employers are the direct beneficiaries [S5][S6].

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: The bill requires employers to keep group health coverage in force during a worker's leave, keeping premium revenue flowing while the worker is out — and the worker keeps insurance at the moment of a birth or serious illness [S5][S6].

School districts and private elementary and secondary schools are covered, but with special rules: limits on intermittent leave for teachers, required leave until the end of an academic term in some cases, and reduced liability for good-faith mistakes [S5][S6].
